question: On which dimensions does the THumB protocol score an image caption?
answer: Precision and recall, plus penalties for fluency, conciseness and inclusive language; the overall score averages precision and recall before the penalties.
key_facts: penalties for fluency, conciseness and inclusive language

question: According to the THumB study, which automatic metric correlates better with human judgments than text-only metrics?

evidence.phrase: better correlates with human judgments than conventional

answer: CLIPScore (CLIP-S), which uses image features; the authors say it is more sensitive to recall.
key_facts: CLIPScore (CLIP-S) correlates better with human judgments than text-only metrics

question: How many pairwise caption battles does CapArena contain, and how do the top models compare with humans?
answer: Over 6000 battles with human preference votes; leading models such as GPT-4o are comparable to or even surpass human-level captions.
key_facts: top models such as GPT-4o match or surpass human-level captions

question: Which LLMs did the ranking-and-fusion captioning paper try for the fusion stage?
answer: Davinci, Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct.

question: What is sentence simplification in the paper 'Let there be a clock on the beach', and why do the authors do it?
answer: Removing adjectives attached to objects in captions (e.g. 'A small black cat ... an old table' becomes 'A cat ... a table'), because the adjectives may not hold when the object is swapped and it adds sentence variation.
key_facts: removes adjectives attached to objects in captions
adjectives may not hold when the object is swapped

question: What is the PAO-EvalBias dataset and how large is it?
answer: A dataset for studying gender bias in caption metrics: 92,049 images of people across 88 professions, 52 activities and 39 objects.
key_facts: built to study gender bias in evaluation metrics

question: How many people did the racial bias study annotate in COCO, and with which attributes?
answer: 28,315 people, annotated with perceived gender and skin color (after IRB approval).

question: What does the control value do in HallE-Control?
answer: A single continuous parameter at inference: -1 makes the model use only visually grounded objects, +1 allows more imagination in the caption.
key_facts: one continuous parameter set at inference

question: Which dataset was SPECS trained on?
answer: ShareGPT-4V, about 1.2 million synthetic high-quality image-caption pairs.

question: Which open relation extraction method does the Focus! news captioning paper use?
answer: OpenNRE (Han et al., 2019), to find relations between pairs of named entities in the article.

question: Which spatial relationship categories does the Image Transformer use between image regions?
answer: Parent, neighbor and child.

question: Into which three categories does the 2018 deep learning captioning survey divide captioning methods, and which one does it focus on?
answer: Template-based, retrieval-based and novel caption generation; it focuses on novel caption generation with deep learning.
key_facts: focuses on novel caption generation with deep learning

question: Which Indonesian image captioning datasets are listed in the multilingual survey of attention-based models?
answer: Flickr8k Bahasa, FEEH-ID and an Indonesian Flickr8k (in the results table); the survey covers Indonesian among its languages on page 3.

question: How is F-CLIPScore computed?
answer: It extracts the nouns of a caption and averages the CLIPScore of the whole sentence with the CLIPScore of each noun.
key_facts: extracts the nouns of a caption
averages the CLIPScore of the whole sentence and of each noun

question: Which attention mechanism and which evaluation metrics does the 'Beyond RNNs' benchmark use?
answer: Bahdanau (additive) attention; BLEU, METEOR, GLEU and WER on MS-COCO.

question: Why do several papers argue that standard metrics such as BLEU or CIDEr are not enough to evaluate captions?
answer: SPECS: n-gram metrics fail to capture semantic correctness, especially for long captions. THumB: most automatic metrics rate machine captions above human ones, the opposite of human judgment. CapArena: metric biases make model rankings inconsistent.
key_facts: SPECS: n-gram metrics miss semantic correctness, especially in long captions
THumB: automatic metrics rate machine captions above human ones, unlike humans
CapArena: metric biases make model rankings inconsistent

question: What different explanations do the papers give for why vision-language models hallucinate objects?
answer: Hyper-detailed captioning: models rely more on their own generated text as captions get longer. F-CLIPScore: the vision encoder's capacity is not necessarily the main cause. HallE-Control: descriptions at a finer granularity than the vision module can ground. Clock on the beach: frequent object co-occurrence in the data. ROPE: models hallucinate more when focusing on several objects, and hallucination follows object class distribution, salience and frequency (shortcuts and spurious correlations).
key_facts: longer captions make models rely on their own generated text (hyper-detailed captioning)
vision encoder capacity is not necessarily the main cause (F-CLIPScore)
details finer than the vision module can ground (HallE-Control)
frequent object co-occurrence in the data (clock on the beach)
ROPE: more hallucination with multiple objects; object class distribution, salience and frequency drive it (shortcuts and spurious correlations)

question: Which papers use the CHAIR metric to measure object hallucination, and what do they say about it?
answer: Clock on the beach reports CHAIRs and CHAIRi; HallE-Control compares CHAIR with its own GPT-4 assisted CCEval for detailed captions.
key_facts: clock on the beach reports CHAIRs and CHAIRi
HallE-Control compares CHAIR with its GPT-4 assisted CCEval

question: What weaknesses of CLIPScore do the papers point out?
answer: Gender bias (it can favour stereotyped captions), weak object-level granularity (F-CLIPScore adds noun-level scores), and weak handling of long detailed captions (SPECS adds specificity).

question: How do the papers in the collection study social bias in image captioning?
answer: One studies racial and intersectional bias in COCO captions using manual skin color and gender annotations; the other studies gender bias in model-based evaluation metrics with PAO-EvalBias and proposes combining model-based and n-gram metrics.
key_facts: racial and intersectional bias in COCO captions with manual skin color and gender annotations
gender bias in model-based evaluation metrics with PAO-EvalBias

question: Which papers use CLIP as part of their own proposed method, rather than only citing or evaluating it?
answer: Required: Focus! (uses CLIP to localize visually grounded entities), SPECS (modifies CLIP with a specificity objective) and F-CLIPScore (builds on CLIPScore). Also acceptable, not required: the gender bias paper's proposed metric combines CLIPScore with n-gram metrics, and CapArena filters its test set with CLIP features. Wrong: THumB, which only evaluates CLIPScore.
key_facts: Focus! uses CLIP to localize visually grounded entities
SPECS modifies CLIP with a specificity objective

question: Which papers use a GPT-4 model as a tool in their method or evaluation?

evidence.phrase: we use GPT-4o to evaluate captions

answer: HallE-Control (CCEval is GPT-4 assisted), CapArena (GPT-4o as the judge) and the hyper-detailed captioning paper (uses GPT-4o to evaluate captions). ROPE only tests GPT-4V as a subject, and SPECS only mentions GPT-4-based metrics, so they do not count.
key_facts: Hyper-detailed captioning: uses GPT-4o to evaluate captions
